description: V2 recommendation library keyed to DOC-151 question IDs. Stub entries generated from assessment questions; refine per DOC-153.

templates.title: Establish centralized workforce identity and authentication
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate user authentication is not fully managed through a centralized identity platform. This finding reflects self-reported assessment information, not an independent technical audit of every system.

Recommended action: Inventory business applications that authenticate users separately. Select or strengthen a primary identity provider for workforce sign-in. Federate or consolidate high-value applications where practical, and define an ownership model for identity administration. Ensure leavers and role changes are processed from the same source of truth.

Expected outcome: Identity administration becomes more consistent, access changes are easier to execute correctly, and security controls such as MFA and password policy can be applied more uniformly.

Implementation considerations: Plan application-by-application cutover to avoid locking users out of line-of-business systems. Confirm licensing, directory sync, and break-glass admin accounts before enforcing centralized sign-in. Coordinate with any existing MSP or internal IT so current support processes remain workable.
templates.businessImpact: Without a central identity platform, account provisioning, access removal, and password policy become inconsistent across systems. That increases the chance of leftover access after role changes or departures, raises help-desk overhead, and makes it harder to contain unauthorized access if credentials are misused.

templates.title: Require multi-factor authentication for privileged and business-critical access
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate multi-factor authentication (MFA) is not consistently required for privileged accounts and business-critical systems. This is based on assessment answers, not a verified penetration test.

Recommended action: Identify privileged roles and systems that handle finance, email, remote access, cloud admin, and customer data. Enforce MFA for those accounts first, then expand to remaining workforce access as capacity allows. Prefer phishing-resistant methods where practical for administrators. Document exception handling and recovery procedures for lost authenticators.

Expected outcome: Credential theft alone becomes less likely to grant immediate access to high-impact systems, reducing the probability and blast radius of account-takeover incidents.

Implementation considerations: Start with privileged and remote-access paths to limit business disruption. Communicate rollout timing, enroll backup factors, and retain a controlled break-glass process. Align MFA policy with the identity platform already in use wherever possible.
templates.businessImpact: Password-only access to admin accounts and critical systems is a common path to ransomware, fraud, and data theft. For an SMB, a single compromised privileged credential can interrupt operations, expose customer or financial data, and create costly recovery work.

templates.title: Eliminate shared credentials in favor of individual user accounts
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate employees may still rely on shared credentials rather than individual accounts for some systems. This reflects reported practices, not a completed credential audit of every application.

Recommended action: Inventory systems that use shared usernames or passwords. Create individual accounts with appropriate roles, migrate users, retire shared credentials, and store any unavoidable service accounts in a controlled secret store with limited ownership. Update onboarding and offboarding checklists accordingly.

Expected outcome: Access activity can be attributed to a person, offboarding becomes more reliable, and the organization reduces the risk that one shared password unlocks broad business access.

Implementation considerations: Some legacy applications only support a single login—document those exceptions, compensate with monitoring or network controls where needed, and schedule replacement or upgrade when practical. Coordinate password changes carefully to avoid downtime.
templates.businessImpact: Shared logins remove personal accountability, complicate offboarding, and make it difficult to investigate misuse. When several people share one password, a single disclosure can expose multiple business functions and extend unauthorized access after someone leaves.

templates.title: Separate privileged administrator accounts from everyday user accounts
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate administrators may not use separate privileged accounts for elevated tasks. This is assessment-reported and should be confirmed during remediation discovery.

Recommended action: Issue dedicated privileged accounts for administration of servers, cloud tenants, firewalls, and identity systems. Require MFA on those accounts, prohibit their use for day-to-day email and browsing, and limit standing privileges where just-in-time elevation is available. Review who holds privileged roles quarterly.

Expected outcome: Everyday account compromise is less likely to yield immediate administrative control, improving containment options and reducing privileged misuse risk.

Implementation considerations: Establish clear naming, vaulting, and break-glass procedures before disabling shared admin habits. Train administrators on when to elevate. Avoid creating unmanaged local admin sprawl as a substitute.
templates.businessImpact: When administrators use the same account for email and privileged work, routine phishing or malware on a daily workstation can escalate to full system control. That elevates operational disruption risk and increases the cost of containment after an incident.

templates.title: Document and operate a joiner–mover–leaver access process
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate a documented joiner, mover, and leaver process is incomplete or missing. Findings are based on assessment responses rather than an HR or directory audit.

Recommended action: Define standard steps for hire, role change, and termination covering account creation, approvals, group membership, MFA enrollment, and timely disablement. Assign owners between HR/operations and IT, use checklists or tickets as the system of record, and measure time-to-revoke for leavers.

Expected outcome: Access more closely matches current job needs, departed users are disabled promptly, and audits or investigations have a clearer trail of who approved what.

Implementation considerations: Keep the process lightweight for SMB scale—simple checklists often outperform unused complex workflows. Integrate with the identity platform and ticketing tools already in place. Pilot with one department before company-wide enforcement.
templates.businessImpact: Without a defined lifecycle process, new hires may receive inconsistent access, role changes leave excess permissions in place, and departed users retain accounts. That creates avoidable security exposure and recurring administrative cleanup for owners and IT providers.

templates.title: Apply least-privilege access aligned to job roles
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate users may not be limited to the access required for their jobs. This is a self-reported maturity indicator, not proof of a specific data exposure.

Recommended action: Define role-based access baselines for common job functions. Review high-risk applications (finance, email admin, file shares, line-of-business systems) and remove unnecessary rights. Prefer group-based assignment over one-off exceptions, and require approval for elevated access.

Expected outcome: Fewer people can reach sensitive systems by default, which reduces blast radius and clarifies ownership of exceptions.

Implementation considerations: Expect negotiation with department leads about "convenience" access. Phase reviews by application criticality. Preserve emergency access paths that are monitored and time-bounded rather than permanent broad rights.
templates.businessImpact: Broad or inherited permissions increase the damage from mistakes, insider misuse, or stolen credentials. Excess access also creates compliance and customer-trust concerns when staff can reach data unrelated to their role.

templates.title: Enforce modern password and authentication policies centrally
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate password requirements may not be centrally enforced using modern practices. This reflects assessment answers, not a password-strength audit of all accounts.

Recommended action: Standardize policy in the primary identity provider: suitable length, protection against known breached passwords where available, sensible lockout/throttling, and MFA as the primary control rather than frequent forced rotation alone. Align federated apps to inherit these controls and retire conflicting local policies where possible.

Expected outcome: Authentication strength becomes more consistent across systems, reducing weak-password exposure and simplifying support.

Implementation considerations: Communicate changes to staff before enforcement. Avoid abrupt lockouts on shared or service accounts—inventory them first. Coordinate with applications that cannot inherit IdP policy so compensating controls are documented.
templates.businessImpact: Weak or inconsistent password rules across systems increase the likelihood of credential stuffing and reuse attacks. Fragmented policy also raises help-desk load and creates uneven protection between critical and secondary applications.

templates.title: Secure remote access with strong authentication and encryption
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate remote access may not be consistently secured with strong authentication and encryption. This is assessment-reported and should be validated against current VPN, RDP, and cloud remote-access configurations during remediation.

Recommended action: Inventory remote access methods (VPN, RDP gateways, cloud admin portals, vendor connections). Require MFA, disable unused exposure, enforce encrypted transport, restrict source networks where practical, and replace legacy direct RDP-to-Internet patterns with hardened gateways or modern remote-access controls.

Expected outcome: Remote work and vendor support continue with a lower likelihood that Internet-facing access alone yields easy account or session takeover.

Implementation considerations: Schedule changes during maintenance windows. Maintain out-of-band recovery access for administrators. Coordinate with any third-party support providers who rely on remote entry so their access is intentional and logged.
templates.businessImpact: Exposed or weakly protected remote access is a frequent entry point for ransomware and unauthorized data access. For distributed or hybrid teams, insecure remote paths can interrupt operations and create significant recovery costs.

templates.title: Review user permissions on a recurring schedule
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate user permissions are not reviewed periodically in a reliable way. This finding is based on reported process maturity, not a completed entitlement scan.

Recommended action: Establish a lightweight quarterly (or semiannual) access review for critical systems and privileged groups. Provide managers with simple membership lists, capture attestations, and remove access that is no longer needed. Track overdue reviews.

Expected outcome: Excess access is pruned regularly, improving accountability and reducing long-lived unnecessary privileges.

Implementation considerations: Focus first on privileged roles, finance systems, and shared mailboxes/files. Keep reviews short enough that managers complete them. Automate exports from the identity platform where possible.
templates.businessImpact: Permissions accumulate over time as people change roles. Without periodic review, dormant access increases unauthorized-use risk and makes investigations slower when something goes wrong.

templates.title: Assign clear ownership for identity and access management
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate responsibility for identity and access management may not be clearly assigned. This is an organizational finding from the assessment, not a technical vulnerability claim.

Recommended action: Name a primary owner (and backup) for identity platform administration, access approvals, and joiner–mover–leaver execution. Document decision rights versus the IT provider or MSP. Include identity topics in a recurring operations review.

Expected outcome: Ownership clarity improves response time for access changes and gives leadership a single point of accountability for identity risk.

Implementation considerations: Ownership can sit with an internal manager supported by an external provider; the key is documented responsibility. Avoid distributing admin rights widely as a substitute for ownership.
templates.businessImpact: When nobody owns identity administration, provisioning and revocation become ad hoc. Gaps show up during employee changes, audits, and incidents—creating avoidable downtime and unclear accountability between leadership and IT support.

templates.title: Implement monitoring for security-relevant system events
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate systems are not adequately monitored for security events. This reflects reported capability, not confirmation that a specific incident was missed.

Recommended action: Define high-value log sources (identity sign-ins, email security, endpoints, firewalls, servers, backups). Enable alerting for suspicious sign-in, malware detections, and privileged changes. Ensure someone is accountable for triage during business hours and for after-hours escalation paths appropriate to business risk.

Expected outcome: Suspicious activity is more likely to be noticed while containment is still feasible, reducing the duration and impact of security events.

Implementation considerations: Start with a focused alert set to avoid noise. Confirm log retention and timezone consistency. If a managed detection service is used, clarify which alerts remain the customer's responsibility.
templates.businessImpact: Without monitoring, unauthorized access, malware activity, or failed attack attempts may go unnoticed until downtime or data loss is already underway. Late detection typically increases recovery time and cost for an SMB.

templates.title: Assess and remediate vulnerabilities on a regular schedule
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate vulnerabilities are not assessed regularly. This is an assessment maturity finding and does not by itself prove a specific exploitable flaw is present.

Recommended action: Establish recurring external and/or internal vulnerability scanning for in-scope systems, prioritize remediations by severity and business criticality, and track closure. Include cloud and remote-access assets. Schedule authenticated scans where credentials improve accuracy.

Expected outcome: Known weaknesses are identified and reduced systematically, lowering the likelihood that publicly known exploits disrupt operations.

Implementation considerations: Coordinate scan windows to avoid performance impact on line-of-business systems. Maintain an exception process for risk-accepted findings with owners and review dates. Align remediation with change management.
templates.businessImpact: Unpatched or misconfigured systems are a leading cause of preventable breaches and outages. Without recurring vulnerability assessment, known weaknesses can accumulate across servers, endpoints, and Internet-facing services.

templates.title: Apply security updates promptly across critical systems
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security updates may not be applied promptly. This finding is based on reported practices rather than a verified patch-compliance inventory.

Recommended action: Define patch SLAs by system class (for example, critical Internet-facing and privileged systems first). Use centralized update tooling where available, test high-risk updates when practical, and report compliance to ownership. Include firmware and third-party apps in scope for high-value assets.

Expected outcome: Exposure windows shrink for known vulnerabilities, and update practices become predictable rather than reactive.

Implementation considerations: Balance speed with change risk—emergency patches for actively exploited issues may bypass normal delays. Maintain rollback plans for core systems. Coordinate with application owners who restrict update timing.
templates.businessImpact: Delayed patching leaves known defects available to attackers and can also cause instability when updates pile up. For SMBs, a single unpatched Internet-facing or backup-related system can drive outsized downtime and recovery expense.

templates.title: Deliver recurring security awareness training for employees
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate employees do not consistently receive security awareness training. This is a process finding from the assessment, not evidence of a particular user failure.

Recommended action: Implement a recurring training program covering phishing, credential protection, data handling, and reporting channels. Include new-hire onboarding and at least annual refreshers. Consider periodic simulated phishing only if results are used for coaching rather than punishment.

Expected outcome: Staff are more likely to pause on suspicious messages and report issues early, improving the organization's human layer of defense.

Implementation considerations: Keep modules short and role-relevant. Ensure reporting of suspicious email is easy. Coordinate with leadership so training completion is an expected business habit, not an IT-only initiative.
templates.businessImpact: Many incidents begin with phishing, unsafe downloads, or accidental data sharing. Without regular awareness training, staff are less prepared to recognize social engineering, which increases the likelihood of account compromise and business email fraud.

templates.title: Establish a practical incident response process
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate an incident response process is missing or incomplete. This reflects preparedness maturity from the assessment, not that an incident is currently active.

Recommended action: Document a concise response plan: severity definitions, internal contacts, provider escalation, containment steps for common scenarios (malware, mailbox compromise, lost device), evidence preservation basics, and communication guidelines. Run a brief tabletop exercise annually and update contacts after org changes.

Expected outcome: The organization can respond faster and more consistently under pressure, limiting operational disruption and supporting clearer decision-making.

Implementation considerations: Keep the plan usable under stress—checklists beat long manuals. Store contacts where they are reachable if email is unavailable. Align with cyber-insurance or legal notification expectations if those already apply to the business.
templates.businessImpact: When an incident occurs without a defined response process, teams lose time deciding who to call, what to isolate, and how to communicate. That delay increases downtime, data-loss risk, and confusion for customers and staff.

templates.title: Retain security logs long enough to support investigations
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security logs may not be retained adequately. This is based on assessment responses, not a forensic review of current log stores.

Recommended action: Identify critical log sources and set retention appropriate to business and investigative needs (commonly weeks to months for SMB security-relevant logs, longer for high-value systems where feasible). Protect logs from tampering, confirm time sync, and ensure responsible parties know how to retrieve them.

Expected outcome: Investigations and post-incident reviews have usable history, improving root-cause analysis and confidence in containment.

Implementation considerations: Balance retention cost with value—prioritize identity, email, endpoint, and firewall logs first. Confirm privacy and contractual constraints. If logs are held by a provider, document how the customer requests exports.
templates.businessImpact: Short or inconsistent log retention makes it difficult to determine how an incident started, what was accessed, and whether the issue is fully contained. That uncertainty prolongs recovery and weakens accountability with customers or partners when questions arise.

templates.title: Review technology and security risks on a recurring cadence
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate technology risks are not reviewed periodically in a structured way. This is a governance finding from the assessment.

Recommended action: Schedule a recurring risk review (for example quarterly) covering open security recommendations, major system changes, backup readiness, vendor access, and incidents or near-misses. Capture owners and next actions in a simple register reviewed by business leadership and IT support.

Expected outcome: Risk decisions become intentional, overdue items surface earlier, and technology investment aligns more closely with business exposure.

Implementation considerations: Keep the register short enough to maintain. Tie reviews to existing leadership meetings where possible. Avoid creating a parallel bureaucracy that will not be sustained.
templates.businessImpact: Without periodic risk review, known issues linger, new tools introduce unmanaged exposure, and leadership lacks a clear picture of technology risk relative to business priorities. That leads to reactive spending and surprise outages or incidents.

templates.title: Include third-party and vendor access in security risk decisions
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate third-party risk may not be considered consistently. This is an assessment-reported governance gap, not an allegation against a specific vendor.

Recommended action: Inventory vendors with access to systems or sensitive data. For material providers, review access paths, require MFA where applicable, remove dormant accounts, and capture basic security expectations in onboarding/offboarding. Revisit access when contracts change.

Expected outcome: External access becomes intentional and reviewable, reducing lingering vendor privileges and clarifying responsibilities when a provider incident occurs.

Implementation considerations: Proportionate effort matters—deep questionnaires are unnecessary for every small tool. Focus on vendors with privileged access, financial data, or production system reach.
templates.businessImpact: Vendors and SaaS platforms often hold sensitive data or privileged remote access. If third-party risk is ignored, a provider weakness or leftover vendor account can disrupt operations or expose information outside the company's direct control.

templates.title: Assign clear ownership for security operations responsibilities
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security ownership may not be clearly assigned. This is an organizational finding from the assessment.

Recommended action: Designate a business-side owner for security outcomes and document which tasks are performed internally versus by an IT provider. Clarify who approves exceptions, who is contacted during incidents, and how recommendations are prioritized. Review the RACI when providers change.

Expected outcome: Accountability is explicit, reducing dropped tasks and speeding decisions when security issues arise.

Implementation considerations: Ownership does not require a full-time CISO for most SMBs; a named manager plus provider support is often enough if responsibilities are written down.
templates.businessImpact: Unclear security ownership leads to missed alerts, delayed patching decisions, and confusion during incidents. Leadership may assume "IT handles it" while providers assume the customer owns risk acceptance—leaving gaps that only appear under pressure.

templates.title: Continuously improve security practices based on incidents and reviews
templates.description:
Finding: Assessment responses indicate security practices are not continuously improved in a deliberate way. This reflects reported maturity, not a grade on any single control.

Recommended action: After incidents, near-misses, audits, or quarterly reviews, capture a small set of improvement actions with owners and due dates. Revisit policies, alerting, and training content when recurring issues appear. Track completion in the same register used for technology risk review.

Expected outcome: Security effort stays aligned to real weaknesses over time rather than one-time projects that slowly decay.

Implementation considerations: Limit work-in-progress—few completed improvements beat a long unfinished list. Review closed actions in leadership meetings to sustain the habit.
templates.businessImpact: Static security practices drift as tools, staff, and threats change. Without continuous improvement, the organization repeats the same failures and spends money on controls that no longer match how the business operates.
